problem.title: 6-DOF UAV Quadcopter — PID Altitude Control with ML-Based Self-Tuning
problem.reference: Mien, T. & Tu, T. (2024), "Design and Quality Evaluation of the Position and Attitude Control System for 6-DOF UAV Quadcopter Using Heuristic PID Tuning Methods", International Journal of Robotics and Control Systems, 4(4), 1712-1730. doi:10.31763/ijrcs.v4i4.1594
problem.thesis: Fixed offline-tuned PID degrades under parameter variation and environmental disturbance. Online tuning is required.
tasks: Task 1 — Develop the dynamic mathematical model of the 6-DOF UAV quadcopter in MATLAB and Simulink in terms of state space equations.
Task 2 — Design the altitude control system for the 6-DOF UAV quadcopter using PID control. Requirement: neat description of the tuning methodology; use the best method available.
Task 3 — Generate data from simulation experiments of the altitude control system and train a suitable ML model for self-tuning of PID gains.
Task 4 — Implement the ML model and present test cases with suitable comparisons and merits of the utilised ML model.

parameters._source: Table 1 of the problem statement (given, not chosen)

task1.headline: 12-state model, verified against an independent numerical derivation to 1.6e-12
task1.states: x = [X, Xdot, Y, Ydot, Z, Zdot, phi, phidot, theta, thetadot, psi, psidot]
task1.why_hard: 6 degrees of freedom but only 4 actuators — underactuated. The quadcopter cannot translate sideways directly; it must tilt. This appears in the model as Xddot = g*theta.
control_mapping: U1 = k(w1^2 + w2^2 + w3^2 + w4^2)      total thrust [N]
U2 = k(w4^2 - w2^2)                    roll input, torque = l*U2
U3 = k(w3^2 - w1^2)                    pitch input, torque = l*U3
U4 = b(w1^2 + w3^2 - w2^2 - w4^2)      yaw torque [N.m]

task2.headline: Feedback linearisation makes Zddot = u_z exactly, at any tilt angle
task2.key_equation: U1 = m(g + u_z) / (cos(phi) cos(theta))   =>   Zddot = u_z
task2.zn_argument: For the plant AS SPECIFIED BY TABLE 1, the Ziegler-Nichols ultimate-gain method is DEGENERATE: Table 1 gives no air-resistance coefficients, so Az = 0 and the altitude channel is a pure double integrator. Under P-only control m*s^2 + Kp = 0 has purely imaginary roots for every Kp > 0 - the loop oscillates at any gain, so no unique ultimate gain Ku exists. The open-loop reaction-curve variant also fails: a double integrator has no S-shaped step response. IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION - DO NOT OVERSTATE THIS: Mien & Tu (2024) DO apply ZN successfully to this same quadcopter. Their Eq. (6) includes air resistance, m*z'' + Az*z' + m*g = F, which moves one pole from the origin to -Az/m so a finite Ku exists - they measure kth = 124.99, tau_th = 3.52 s. Neither their Table 1 nor our problem statement gives values for Ax, Ay, Az, so setting them to zero is the only consistent reading of the data we were given. The honest statement is: 'for the plant as specified by Table 1 the ZN ultimate-gain method is degenerate; the reference avoids this because its model retains aerodynamic drag.'
task2.winner_margin: Method D is 6.3x better by ITAE than the next best (0.0840 vs 0.5311)

tilt_test.description: Altitude sag when the quadcopter pitches, holding altitude command constant
tilt_test.comparison: A conventional hover-linearised PID settles about 1.3 cm low at 17 degrees. Ours sags 2 micrometres in the Simulink model — roughly 1/40th the width of a human hair.

task2.why_Ki_zero: Feedback linearisation cancels gravity via feed-forward, so in the nominal case there is no steady-state error for integral action to remove — it would only add overshoot. The optimiser correctly deleted it. The consequence matters: with Ki = 0 the controller is NOT robust to an unknown payload, which is what motivates Task 3.
task2.saturation_note: Peak thrust reaches 20.248 N, exactly the actuator limit, during the initial climb. This is correct behaviour: Method D demands 32.8 m/s^2 while the rotors deliver at most 29.43, so the command clips briefly. Clamping anti-windup prevents integrator windup, which is why overshoot is still only 0.07%.

reference_benchmark._note: All four designs simulated on the identical plant, stepping to the paper's own setpoint z=2.0 m. Their three run as plain PID (their Eq. 27); ours runs feedback-linearised.
reference_benchmark.formula_reproduction: Our implementation of their Eq. (24) ZN and Eq. (25) Tyreus-Luyben formulas reproduces their published Table 2/3 altitude gains to under 4e-5 error.
reference_benchmark.headline: Lowest ITAE of all four - 1.8x better than the best of their three, 36x better than Tyreus-Luyben which their paper concludes is best.
reference_benchmark.validation: Their paper reports Tyreus-Luyben achieving 'steady-state error of less than 1%'. Our simulation of their gains gives 0.592% - inside their stated bound, confirming we reproduced their design correctly.
reference_benchmark.tilt_headline: 253x less altitude sag than their best-rated method under a 17.2 deg pitch step.

task3.headline: The controller is never told the payload mass — it infers it from its own thrust command

framing.what_others_do: Gain scheduling: features = [mass, wind] -> network -> gains. The fatal flaw is that in flight the drone does not know its payload mass. Someone must measure it and type it in. This is a lookup table with a neural network on top.
framing.what_we_do: Response-signature inference: fly 3 s on baseline gains, measure how the aircraft responded, infer the gains from that signature. The network learns the inverse map: observed closed-loop response -> the gains that condition needs.

task3.key_insight: In steady hover, thrust must exactly equal weight. So mean thrust divided by nominal weight IS the mass ratio. The controller reads its own payload off its own thrust command — no extra sensor.

correlations._note: Pearson r, measured across 150 sampled operating conditions

ki_vs_payload._note: The headline physics result. Predicted from theory BEFORE the data existed, then confirmed by independent optimisation.
ki_vs_payload.explanation: Ki is exactly zero at nominal and rises almost linearly with payload excess. Feedback linearisation removes the need for integral action only when the mass is known; with an unknown payload the feed-forward is mis-scaled and leaves a constant offset that only integral action can remove.

fixed_gain_failure._note: Same Task 2 gains, unknown payload. This is the argument for Task 3.

model_comparison._note: Four classes trained on an identical 70/15/15 split, selected on held-out mean R^2. PROVISIONAL - may change with Task 4.
model_comparison.finding: The deepest network scored WORSE than a straight line - 150 samples against ~200 parameters overfits. Held-out model selection caught this.

r2.why: Ki is uniquely determined - a given steady-state error needs a specific integral strength. Many (Kp,Kd) pairs give near-identical cost, so the cost surface has a flat valley and those labels are intrinsically noisy. No model can predict noise.

task3.status: COMPLETE but PROVISIONAL - subject to change based on Task 4 requirements

task4.headline: PENDING
how_it_works: Phase 1 (0 to 3 s): fly on the fixed baseline gains, record the response
At 3 s: compute the 8-feature signature -> network -> predicted gains -> clamp to a safe range -> hand the integrator state over (bumpless transfer)
Phase 2 (3 to 12 s): continue on the predicted gains

three_way_comparison.fixed_pid: the Task 2 baseline — what we are trying to beat
three_way_comparison.oracle: gains optimised directly for that exact condition — the theoretical ceiling. Uses multi-start (5 seeds including non-zero Ki) because a single search from the Ki=0 baseline gets trapped brute-forcing with a huge Kp.

limitations: Envelope-bound: valid for mass x1.0-2.4 and wind +/-1 N. Outside that the network extrapolates and should not be trusted.
Needs a 3-second identification window before it can adapt; during that window performance equals the baseline.
Trained entirely in simulation, so it inherits every modelling error — rigid airframe, no blade flapping, instantaneous motor response, no ground effect.

No formal stability guarantee. The network could in principle output destabilising gains, which is why the output is clamped. A Lyapunov-based adaptive scheme would give guarantees a black-box regressor cannot.

Kp and Kd are weakly predicted because their labels are intrinsically noisy — the cost surface has a flat valley in those directions, so the optimiser lands anywhere along it. Ki, which is uniquely determined and which drives the performance gain, predicts well.
Scope is altitude control, as Task 2 specifies. Position and attitude loops are the stated next step.
